name: Paro
tagline: Bhutan's front door, with the Tiger's Nest on its cliff
meta_description: Paro, Bhutan: Tiger's Nest hike times and fees, Rinpung Dzong, Kyichu Lhakhang, where to stay at every budget, and honest costs for Indian travellers.
summary: Paro is the broad valley at 2,250 m that holds Bhutan's only international airport, the Rinpung Dzong and, 10 km up the valley, the Tiger's Nest on its cliff. Most trips start or end here. Give it two to three nights: one full day for Taktsang, one for the dzong, museum and Kyichu Lhakhang.
intro: Paro is where most visitors first touch Bhutan, either stepping off a plane that has threaded between ridges into the 2,235 m airstrip or arriving by road from Phuentsholing via Chhuzom. The valley is wide by Bhutanese standards, with red rice paddies, apple orchards and farmhouses painted with lotus and dragon motifs. The town itself is one main street of painted wooden shopfronts, a few cafes and handicraft stores, with the Paro Chhu running below.

The landmarks sit close together. Rinpung Dzong, consecrated in 1646 by the Zhabdrung, rises above a covered cantilever bridge. On the hill behind it the round watchtower of Ta Dzong, built in 1649, has housed the National Museum since 1968. North of town, Kyichu Lhakhang is one of the two oldest temples in the country. At the head of the valley the ruins of Drukgyel Dzong, burnt in the early 1950s, are being rebuilt.

Then there is Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest, at 3,120 m on a cliff about 900 m above the valley floor. It is the hike everyone remembers. We suggest doing it on your last full day, after a few nights at 2,200–2,300 m, when your legs and lungs have adjusted. Paro also makes the base for the drive over Chele La to Haa and the start of the Druk Path trek to Thimphu.
facts: Tiger's Nest, Rinpung Dzong, National Museum, Paro Tshechu

highlights.title: Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest
highlights.text: A 4–6 hour return hike from the car park at about 2,600 m to the monastery at 3,120 m. The trail passes a water-driven prayer wheel, a cafeteria viewpoint and a 60 m waterfall. Phones and cameras are deposited before you enter the shrines.

highlights.title: Rinpung Dzong
highlights.text: The 'fortress on a heap of jewels' houses Paro's monk body and district offices. Walk down to the covered cantilever bridge below it. Scenes from the 1993 film Little Buddha were shot here, and the Paro Tshechu is held on the Deyangkha ground beside it.

highlights.title: National Museum in Ta Dzong
highlights.text: The 17th-century watchtower above the dzong was converted into the National Museum in 1968 and holds more than 3,000 works of Bhutanese art, from bronzes and thangkas to masks and textiles. Entry is about Nu 300.

highlights.title: Kyichu Lhakhang
highlights.text: Said to have been founded in 659 by the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, this is one of Bhutan's oldest temples. Two orange trees in the courtyard are said to fruit all year. Come at 8 am to see elderly villagers turning the prayer wheels.

highlights.title: Drukgyel Dzong
highlights.text: Built in 1649 to mark victory over a Tibetan invasion and nearly destroyed by fire in the early 1950s, the 'fortress of the victorious Drukpas' is being rebuilt after a 2016 announcement. On clear days Jomolhari shows above it.

field_notes.fact: Taktsang was rebuilt after a fire on 19 April 1998 damaged the main building and killed a monk; the restoration, overseen by the government and the fourth king, cost about Nu 135 million and was completed in 2005.
Before dawn on the last day of the Paro Tshechu, a giant thongdrel of Guru Rinpoche's eight manifestations is unrolled on the dzong wall and taken down early so that sunlight never falls on it.
Flights into Paro are allowed only under visual flying conditions and in daylight, and the approach passes peaks of about 5,500 m, so only a small number of specially certified pilots operate here.

local_word.meaning: tiger's lair; one of 13 such caves linked to Guru Rinpoche

costs: Nu 1,000–2,000 (DoT list shows Nu 2,000; check current status)

how_to_reach.text: Paro International Airport is 6 km from town. Drukair and Bhutan Airlines have flown from Delhi, Kolkata, Bagdogra, Guwahati, Kathmandu and Bangkok; routes and fares change, so check current status before you travel.

Public buses link Paro with Thimphu and Phuentsholing, but tourists must travel with a licensed guide beyond the first checkpoint, so most visitors use the operator's vehicle. Ask your operator if a public-bus leg with your guide is possible.
Phuentsholing to Paro is about 150 km and 5–6 hours via Chhuzom. Thimphu to Paro is about 55 km and 1 h 15 min. Haa to Paro over Chele La is about 65 km and 2.5–3 hours.

where_to_stay: Saver travellers use the simple tourist-certified hotels along the main street and the airport road, with doubles around ₹2,500–4,500 and heating that varies, so ask. Comfort travellers do well at Zhiwa Ling Heritage near Satsam Chorten, a hand-built Bhutanese-owned hotel with a temple inside, or at Le Méridien Paro Riverfront on the river. Signature options are COMO Uma Paro on a pine-covered hill above town and Amankora's Paro lodge, set in a blue pine forest near the ruins of Drukgyel Dzong.
tips: Do the Taktsang hike on your last full day in Bhutan, after two or three nights at 2,200 m or higher.
Start the hike by 8 am; the shrines close for lunch around 12 to 2 pm.
Carry your entry permit copy and wear long sleeves and trousers or a long skirt for temples and dzongs.
Ask for a left-side window seat when flying into Paro from Delhi or Kathmandu for the high peaks.
Paro Tshechu dates sell out hotels in Paro and Thimphu; book three to four months ahead.

experiences.title: Hike to Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest
experiences.image_query: Paro Taktsang Tiger's Nest monastery cliff
experiences.summary: The classic Bhutan day: a steady climb of about 500 m from the car park to the cafeteria viewpoint, then on to the monastery at 3,120 m, with a final drop and climb of roughly 700 steps past a 60 m waterfall.
body: The trail starts at a car park at about 2,600 m, 10 km north of Paro town. A water-powered prayer wheel turns in a stream near the start. The first section climbs through blue pine forest on a broad, dusty mule track. After about 1.5–2 hours you reach the cafeteria, which faces the monastery across the ravine and serves tea, biscuits and a simple buffet lunch. Many people stop here, and that is a fine choice for children or anyone who feels the altitude.

From the cafeteria the path climbs to a viewpoint level with the monastery, then descends a long flight of steps to a bridge over the waterfall and climbs again to the gate. Lockers take cameras, phones and bags; photography is not allowed inside. A guide is required to enter, and the shrines usually close for a midday break. Inside, the main cave is linked with Padmasambhava's meditation and is opened to the public only once a year.

Ponies can carry you uphill as far as the cafeteria; they do not go down, because the descent is hard on their legs and riders are thrown forward. Wear shoes with grip, carry 1 litre of water and a light jacket, and go slowly: the monastery sits above 3,000 m. Talk to your doctor before the hike if you have heart or lung conditions. Return the same way, which takes about 2 hours.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Tiger's Nest hike?
faqs.a: It is moderate: about 4–5 km each way with roughly 500–600 m of climbing to the monastery at 3,120 m, plus steep steps near the end. Fit adults take 2.5–3 hours up and 2 hours down. Go slowly, drink water and turn back at the cafeteria if you feel dizzy or breathless.

faqs.q: Can children and seniors do the hike?
faqs.a: Many do. Children over about eight usually manage with breaks, and seniors can ride a pony to the cafeteria and decide there whether to continue. The final steps cannot be done on horseback. If you have heart, lung or knee problems, talk to your doctor before you go.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Taktsang?
faqs.a: No. Cameras and phones go into lockers at the entrance and photography is banned inside all shrines. The best photos are from the cafeteria and the viewpoint opposite the monastery, ideally in morning light before 10 am.

experiences.title: Rinpung Dzong and the National Museum on foot
experiences.summary: Walk from the town across the covered cantilever bridge, up through the dzong's courtyards and on to the round Ta Dzong watchtower that now holds the National Museum, then back down through farm lanes.
body: Start at the main street and cross the Paro Chhu on the covered wooden bridge below Rinpung Dzong. The dzong was consecrated in 1646 after the Zhabdrung received an older fortress from the descendants of a local lama, and it now houses the district monk body in one courtyard and Paro's administration in the other. You enter through a steep stone ramp and a heavy wooden gate. Inside, look for the cosmic mandala paintings in the gate passage and the tall central tower.

Above the dzong, Ta Dzong was built in 1649 as a watchtower and became the National Museum of Bhutan in 1968. Its collection of more than 3,000 works spans bronzes, thangkas, festival masks, arms and textiles. The museum building has been under renovation in some years, with displays moved to a nearby block, so ask your guide what is open; check current status before you travel.

From the museum, walk back down past houses with painted windows to the Deyangkha ground beside the dzong, where the Paro Tshechu's masked dances are held each spring. The full loop is about 3 km with 150 m of climbing. Dress modestly: long sleeves and long trousers or skirt, no hats inside. Your guide will wear a ceremonial scarf to enter the dzong.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Rinpung Dzong?
faqs.a: Tourists can usually visit in the morning and afternoon on working days, with a lunch break. The Department of Tourism fee list shows 9 am–12 pm and 2–5 pm. Hours change during festivals and official events, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a dress code for the dzong?
faqs.a: Yes. Wear long sleeves and full-length trousers or a long skirt, remove hats and sunglasses, and avoid shorts, sleeveless tops and flip-flops. Bhutanese wear the gho or kira with a ceremonial scarf; tourists are not required to wear national dress.

faqs.q: Can I photograph inside the dzong?
faqs.a: You can photograph the courtyards and exterior, but not inside temples and shrine rooms. Ask your guide when unsure, and do not point cameras at monks during prayers without a nod of permission.

experiences.title: Morning prayer wheels at Kyichu Lhakhang
experiences.summary: One of Bhutan's two oldest temples, a few minutes north of Paro town, where villagers walk circuits and spin prayer wheels in the early morning. Quiet, short and easy to fit before a Taktsang or Haa day.
body: Kyichu Lhakhang is said to have been built in 659 by the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo as one of 108 temples raised to pin down a demoness who was blocking the spread of Buddhism. The historian Karma Phuntsho has noted that for many Bhutanese the country's history effectively begins with this story. Its twin in Bhutan is Jambay Lhakhang in Bumthang. Guru Rinpoche is believed to have visited and hidden treasures here.

The complex has two parts: the old Jowo temple and a Guru temple added in 1971 by Queen Kesang Choden Wangchuck. Two orange trees in the courtyard are said to bear fruit all year. Early morning is the time to come: elderly villagers walk clockwise around the walls, spinning the row of prayer wheels and murmuring mantras.

Walk with them, always clockwise, and keep your voice low. Photography is not allowed inside. The temple is about 5 minutes by car from town, or a flat 3 km walk along the valley road. Pair it with breakfast in Paro and a drive up to the Taktsang car park, or with an early start over Chele La to Haa.

faqs.a: Tradition dates it to 659, built by the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo as one of 108 border-taming temples. It has been restored several times, including in 1836–38, and a second temple was added in 1971. It is counted among the oldest temples in Bhutan.

faqs.q: How do I get to Kyichu Lhakhang?
faqs.a: It lies about 3 km north of Paro town on the road towards Drukgyel Dzong and Taktsang. Your guide's vehicle takes 5 minutes; walking takes about 40 minutes on a flat road. Most visitors combine it with the Tiger's Nest hike.

faqs.q: What is the right way to walk around a temple?
faqs.a: Always clockwise, keeping the temple on your right. Spin prayer wheels clockwise too. Remove shoes and hats where asked, do not point your feet at altars, and drop a small note in the offering box if you wish.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Paro?
faqs.a: Two to three nights. One day for the Tiger's Nest hike, one for Rinpung Dzong, the National Museum and Kyichu Lhakhang, and an optional day trip over Chele La to Haa. If you fly in, spend your first nights in Thimphu or Punakha and come back to Paro at the end for Taktsang.

Yes. At about 2,250 m, Paro is high enough that some people feel short of breath on stairs on day one, but low enough to adjust in a day or two. Save the Taktsang hike to 3,120 m for later in the trip. Talk to your doctor if you have heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Tiger's Nest?
faqs.a: The Department of Tourism's monument fee list shows Nu 2,000 for Taktsang, while some operators quote Nu 1,000. The ngultrum is at par with the rupee. Fees are paid on site or through your operator. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can Indians fly into Paro and get a permit on arrival?
faqs.a: Yes, as we understand it. Indian nationals with a passport or voter ID can get the entry permit at Paro airport, paying the ₹1,200 per night SDF. Applying online in advance through your operator is faster. Your permit must list districts beyond Paro and Thimphu that you will visit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Paro?
faqs.a: March to May for flowering orchards, rhododendrons and the Paro Tshechu, and October to November for clear skies and harvest colours. Winter is clear and cold with low prices. July and August are rainy and the Taktsang trail turns muddy.

Yes, several bank ATMs on the main street and at the airport, though foreign and Indian cards do not always work. Indian rupees are accepted widely at par in shops and restaurants. Carry ₹100–500 notes and some cash for monument fees and tips.

faqs.q: What does a day in Paro cost on a budget?
faqs.a: For an Indian traveller sharing a guide and vehicle with three others: SDF ₹1,200, a simple hotel on twin share ₹1,500–2,000, meals ₹700–1,000, a share of guide and car ₹1,500–2,500, and entry fees. Plan ₹5,000–7,000 per person per day, more on Taktsang day.

Paro is a small, quiet town and is generally safe in the evening. Streets are dark outside the centre, so carry a torch, and watch for stray dogs, which bark at night. Restaurants close early, often by 9 pm, outside the bigger hotels.

faqs.q: Can I visit Haa from Paro in a day?
faqs.a: Yes. Haa is about 65 km over Chele La at 3,988 m, roughly 2.5–3 hours each way. Leave early for clear views of Jomolhari from the pass, visit the White and Black temples in Haa and return by evening. Haa must be on your permit, and the pass can see snow from December to March; check current status before you travel.
